sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: U.S. military government
sources.note: XXIV Corps, government south of the 38th parallel, conflicts over Korean governing bodies, administrative Koreanization, and the 15 August 1948 endpoint.

sources.title: MacArthur Proclamation No. 1 for Korea
sources.note: Contemporaneous proclamation asserting military control south of 38 degrees north and naming English as the official language of military control.

sources.title: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1945 occupation directive
sources.note: U.S. instructions on administration, food, schools, archives, utilities, public health, censorship, and displaced people; a policy document rather than an outcome survey.

sources.title: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1947 Korea policy memorandum
sources.note: U.S. assessment of political antagonism, economic crisis, education, relief, and self-government; preserve its official perspective.

sources.title: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1948 election and transfer memorandum
sources.note: UN-observed election in the accessible area, transfer of functions, troop questions, and southern dependence on northern electric power.

sources.title: Foreign Relations of the United States, 1949 military-government termination
sources.note: Formal 15 August 1948 termination, later transfer work, and separate troop-withdrawal chronology.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: curriculum after liberation
sources.note: School reopening, Korean history restoration, textbook replacement, provisional syllabi, and incomplete decolonization through 1954.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: public health after liberation
sources.note: Health-administration sequence, shortages, 1948 contraction, later reorganization, and aid-supported centers and clinics.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: rice supply and hunger
sources.note: Shortage, free-market reversal, collection and rationing, black markets, return migration, cholera, and a March 1946 Daegu school example.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: water, drainage, kitchens, and housing
sources.note: A 79-city water count, weak coverage, damaged drains, wastewater disposal, water carrying, kitchens, and 1954 Jeongneung reconstruction homes.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: wartime refugee life in Busan
sources.note: Teaching page on journeys, scarce camps, makeshift shacks, water queues, dock labor, and street vending; qualitative rather than representative.

sources.title: U.S. Army Center of Military History: South to the Naktong, North to the Yalu
sources.note: Official military history for division, surrender, invasion, early campaigns, refugees, and geography; use critically and pair with civilian sources.

sources.title: U.S. Army Center of Military History: Korean War campaign summary
sources.note: High-level invasion, intervention, armistice-negotiation, and July 1953 ceasefire chronology, not a civilian social history.

sources.title: National Archives: Korean Armistice Agreement
sources.note: Signed 27 July 1953, suspended open hostilities, created a military arrangement and demilitarized zone, and was not a permanent peace treaty.

sources.title: National Archives: Armed Forces Assistance to Korea records schedule
sources.note: Record-series description for Army assistance to hospitals, schools, and public facilities; proves program records, not completed outcomes by itself.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: Korea-U.S. aid agreement
sources.note: December 1948 agreement and transition from occupation relief to state-to-state aid involving food, necessities, medicine, and economic support.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: Jeju 4·3
sources.note: 1947 shooting and strike, 1948 uprising, armed actors, scorched-earth repression, civilian killing, and social crisis, with contested interpretations.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: Yeosu-Suncheon incident
sources.note: October 1948 refusal by the 14th Regiment, revolt, state suppression, civilian killing, and security-state consequences; estimates and labels remain contested.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: land reform
sources.note: Distribution of formerly Japanese-owned land, 1949 law, March 1950 implementation, wartime disruption, falling tenancy, repayment, and pre-sale limits.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: April Revolution
sources.note: Student protests, March 1960 electoral fraud, police violence, wider participation, and Syngman Rhee resignation announcement on 26 April.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: Jin Yeong-suk testament
sources.note: Contemporaneous testament of one middle-school student before joining an April 1960 demonstration; one individual voice, not a collective transcript.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: educational expansion and tent schools
sources.note: Later textbook synthesis of the 6-3-3 system, wartime tent schooling, institutional expansion, and returned specialists.

sources.title: National Archives of Korea: liberation, war, and reconstruction exhibition
sources.note: Archival exhibition with dated photographs and named records on refugees and reconstruction; use individual captions rather than the exhibition title alone.

sources.title: UNHCR Korea: Korea and refugees in history
sources.note: Institutional retrospective on war displacement, UN intervention, and UNKRA; pair its program history with Korean archival evidence.

sources.title: Korean Law Information Center: Constitution of 1948
sources.note: Official enacted Korean text effective 17 July 1948, including Article 1.

sources.title: Korea Legislation Research Institute: Constitution Article 1 in English
sources.note: Official English interface giving the unchanged Article 1 clause; the separate Korean historical-law record establishes its 1948 enactment.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History database: 1950 cleaning campaign speech
sources.note: Government rhetoric on DDT, clothing, bedding, dwellings, latrines, waste, lice, fleas, and bedbugs; evidence of a campaign, not safety or compliance.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean History: GoldStar A-501 radio
sources.note: 1959 A-501 launch, low-voltage design, and imported components; domestic production did not mean every part was Korean.

sources.title: Seoul Metropolitan Archives: tuberculosis control
sources.note: Seoul institutions, planned 1950 BCG vaccination, 1954 estimates, later programs, and acknowledged gaps between law and access.

sources.title: Seoul Sewerage Science Museum: water and sewer history
sources.note: War damage, untreated Cheonggyecheon sewage, 1958 covering work, low 1960 water coverage, and an 83-city count that conflicts with another source.

sources.title: United Nations Security Council report on Korea, 1950
sources.note: Official report of medical teams, immunization, and environmental-sanitation programs in refugee camps; program reporting, not an independent outcome study.

sources.title: United Nations Korean reconstruction report, 1952
sources.note: Official report on relief deliveries, refugees, war sufferers, local destitution, and camp return; institutional reporting with incomplete recipient voices.

proposedOverrides.name: Korea (USA)
proposedOverrides.summary: A simplified southern-Korea atlas layer spanning U.S. military government, the Republic founded in 1948, war, reconstruction, and political change to 1960.

batchIdentityNotes: Korea (USA) is an atlas shorthand for a southern layer, not a sovereign polity, annexation, citizenship, or fifteen-year military government.
U.S. Army military government ended on 15 August 1948; the Republic of Korea continued through the remaining interval.
The geometry projects a later South-Korea-shaped polygon backward, excluding Kaesong and Haeju, leaving sampled Sokcho unowned, and pairing with a northern feature that spills into Dandong.
The 1960 transition to korea-republic-of is direct state continuity, not a fall or newly founded successor.
